title: The organic curve of growth resembles the velocity curve of chemical autocatalysis

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The organic curve of growth resembles the velocity curve of chemical autocatalysis

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The normal curve of growth of an organism closely resembles the velocity curve of an autocatalytic chemical reaction, with a phase of increasing acceleration, a phase in which limiting conditions reduce acceleration, and usually a final phase of retardation and loss of mass; but only a resemblance, not an identity, can yet be asserted.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it is sufficiently clear that the normal “curve of growth” of an organism, in all its general features, very closely resembles the velocity-curve of chemical autocatalysis.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Growth and catalytic action”. Scope: growth of organisms generally

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-27: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.61

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Growth curves are abundant and model comparison is straightforward, but qualitative resemblance has weak discriminating power. Existing data can resolve the pattern in selected taxa, not the claim's organism-wide scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit organismal growth time series with an explicit autocatalytic-reaction velocity model and compare predictive fit against logistic, Gompertz, von Bertalanffy, and flexible spline alternatives. The resemblance is supported only if the autocatalytic shape consistently captures the stated acceleration and retardation phases without being outperformed.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Closely resembles' has no specified goodness-of-fit threshold.

Many unrelated growth models yield similar sigmoid curves.

Available databases often store fitted parameters rather than raw time series.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.8
data adequacy: 0.6
analysis feasibility: 0.75
discriminating power: 0.35
operationalizability: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Open growth trajectories are now abundant enough to score the three phases Thompson describes for many animals. The decision is soft, because he explicitly allows resemblance rather than identity and because several standard growth laws look alike through the middle of life. Terminal mass loss and the contrast with chemical equilibrium are much less well covered than the rising and slowing phases.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare observed size-versus-age curves with the velocity curve of an autocatalytic reaction, asking whether growth shows an accelerating phase, a phase of falling acceleration, and a late phase of slowing or mass loss, and whether the late phase behaves like chemical equilibrium. Sharing those phases while the endpoint is differentiation rather than chemical equilibrium would support resemblance without identity; a growth curve lacking the accelerating phase, or an endpoint that is chemical equilibrium, would refute that qualified claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Logistic, Gompertz and von Bertalanffy curves share the same broad sigmoid shape.

The claim already hedges resemblance against identity, so a moderate misfit is compatible with the wording.

Public trajectories often stop before the late loss of mass.
